title: Elizabeth Ann Seton (1774–1821)
hook: a widowed mother, a convert, a founder of schools, honored as a saint

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden Christians of Japan, the kakure kirishitan, keeping baptism and prayer alive with no priests. Your line was 250 years in secret. Did your small habit happen? Today, a young widow in New York. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

Her husband coughs through the night in a cold stone quarantine building on the coast of Italy, and she is the one nursing him. He is dying of tuberculosis. Their little daughter is with her; the other children are home in New York. She is American, she belongs to the Episcopal Church, and she reads her Bible. When her husband dies, an Italian Catholic family, the Filicchis, take her in. She goes to Mass with them and watches how they pray. Then she sails home a widow, with young children, little money, and a head full of questions. Her name is Elizabeth Ann Seton.
screen: `A QUARANTINE ROOM IN ITALY.` → `A HUSBAND DIES.` → `A CATHOLIC FAMILY TAKES HER IN.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Back in New York, what drew her most was the Eucharist, the Catholic belief that Christ is truly present in the bread at Mass. She wrote about wanting to be near it. She was received into the Catholic Church, and friends and relatives pulled away. Help dried up. Second, the classroom. A widow with children had to earn a living, so she taught. A school she tried in New York struggled. Then she was invited to Baltimore, and there she opened a small school for girls. Later, in a valley at Emmitsburg, Maryland, she started another, where poorer children could learn alongside those who paid. Third, the sisters. Women came to join her, and she founded a religious community, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph's. They began calling her Mother Seton. She did not stop being a mother at home, either; she was raising her own children through all of it, and she grieved the deaths of daughters she loved. Fourth, the saint. The Church canonized her, and Catholic schools across the United States name her as a patron. A teacher, honored as a saint. In the Gospel of Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me." She spent her last years doing that in a schoolroom, one lesson and one child at a time.
screen: `DRAWN BY THE EUCHARIST.` · `A WIDOW WHO TEACHES.` · `THE SISTERS OF CHARITY.` · `A TEACHER CANONIZED.` · then, large: `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Settle, and breathe. Let one teacher come to mind. A schoolteacher, a coach, a grandmother at a kitchen table, a boss who showed you how. Remember one thing they taught you that you still use. Hold their face for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply stay with the gratitude. When the bell rings, you might send them a message, or say their name to someone. The bell holds the time.
Eucharist. The Catholic belief that Christ is truly present in the bread at Mass, the thing that drew Elizabeth Ann Seton into the Catholic Church.
Your line: mother seton. Today, thank one person who taught you something, out loud or in writing, and tell them what it was. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Elizabeth Ann Seton's feast in early January, and Catholic schools often mark it with a Mass and stories of her life; pilgrims visit her shrine at Emmitsburg, Maryland.
